questions.q: Describe what happens when two developers edit the same file and push to a shared Git remote.
questions.m: The first push succeeds. The second fails because the remote has changed. The second developer pulls and merges the first one's changes, then pushes successfully, and both sync again.

questions.q: List three practices that keep code simple and readable.

questions.m: Calculator is a functional interface with one abstract method, calculate(int, int). The lambda has two parameters and returns an int, so it supplies that method's body.

questions.q: Explain why List<Integer> isn't a List<Object>, and how a wildcard fixes the method header.
questions.m: If List<Integer> were a List<Object>, a method could add a String to a list of integers, breaking type safety. Declaring the parameter as List<?> accepts a list of any type without allowing unsafe additions.

questions.q: Give two problems that generics solved.
questions.m: Without generics, reading from a collection needed a cast, and nothing stopped you adding the wrong type, so errors appeared only at run time. Generics remove the cast and check types at compile time.

questions.q: Explain the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions, with one example of each.
questions.m: Checked exceptions are checked at compile time and must be caught or declared, for example IOException. Unchecked exceptions are RuntimeException, Error and their subclasses, which reflect logic errors and aren't enforced by the compiler, for example NullPointerException.

questions.q: In a try with statement1 to statement3, statement2 throws Exception2, which is caught and rethrown. Trace what executes.
questions.m: statement1 runs, statement2 throws, statement3 is skipped. The catch(Exception2) block runs and rethrows. finally runs. Control passes to the caller, so the next statement in the method does not run.

questions.m: Faculty() calls super(), meaning Employee(), which calls this(...), meaning Employee(String), which calls super(), meaning Person(). Person prints (1), Employee(String) prints (2), Employee() prints (3), and Faculty prints (4).

questions.q: Explain why the slides redesign the Employee hierarchy using composition and an interface.
questions.m: Employees differ only in how they're paid, so each Employee has a CompensationModel interface instead of being a subclass. This reduces coupling: a pay rule changes in one class, new capabilities such as retirement plans become new interfaces, and a promotion just calls setCompensationModel.

questions.q: List the conditions for a class to be immutable, and explain why a class with no setters may still be mutable.
questions.m: All fields must be private, there must be no mutator methods, and no accessor may return a reference to a mutable field. Without setters, a getter that returns an array or Date object still lets callers change the internal state, so return a copy instead.

Explain how 100 deposit threads can leave an account with less than 100, and how to fix it.
questions.m: Two threads read the same balance, both add 1, and the second write overwrites the first, so a deposit is lost. This race condition is fixed by making deposit synchronized, or by using a ReentrantLock, so only one thread runs the read-modify-write at a time.

questions.q: Describe a deadlock between two threads and how resource ordering prevents it.
questions.m: Thread 1 holds object1 and waits for object2 while Thread 2 holds object2 and waits for object1, so neither can continue. With resource ordering, both threads must lock object1 before object2, so Thread 2 waits for object1 and no circular wait can form.

questions.q: Compare implementing Runnable with extending Thread.
questions.m: Implementing Runnable keeps the task separate from the thread and leaves the class free to extend another class, though the client must wrap it in a Thread. Extending Thread gives cleaner client code but uses up the single superclass and adds all of Thread's methods to the class.

questions.q: Define idempotency and explain why it matters for REST APIs.
questions.m: A request is idempotent if executing it once or many times has the same effect on the server. Clients may send duplicates after timeouts or network errors, so idempotent operations keep the system stable, and their results can be cached. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST and PATCH are not.

questions.q: Write a GET handler that returns a product by ID, or 404 if it doesn't exist.
questions.m: @GetMapping("/{requestedId}") ResponseEntity<Product> findById(@PathVariable Integer requestedId) { Optional<Product> p = productRepository.findById(requestedId); if (p.isPresent()) return ResponseEntity.ok(p.get()); return ResponseEntity.notFound().build(); }

Explain a CSRF attack and how a CSRF token prevents it.
questions.m: A malicious page makes the victim's browser send a state-changing request, such as a transfer, to a site where they're logged in; the browser attaches the session cookie automatically. A CSRF token is embedded in the real page and must be sent with the request. It isn't sent automatically and SOP stops the attacker reading it, so forged requests fail.

questions.q: Compare CSRF and XSS, with one defence for each.
questions.m: CSRF tricks the browser into sending a request with the user's cookies; it's defended with CSRF tokens or SameSite cookies. XSS gets an attacker's script to run on the victim site, where it can read tokens and cookies; it's defended by escaping or sanitizing external data, a Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies.

questions.q: Describe how JWT authentication works in a Spring API.
questions.m: After a successful login, the server generates a signed JWT containing claims and an expiry and returns it. The client sends it in the Authorization: Bearer header with each request. A JwtFilter validates the signature and expiry and sets the user's authentication before the controller runs. No session is stored, so it is stateless.
